---
title: Command-Line Reference
---

## Basic Usage

```bash
pycmdcheck [OPTIONS] [PATH]
```

`PATH` is the directory to check. It defaults to the current directory, and it
must be a directory.

## What a Run Executes

With no `--check` (or `-c` for short), no `--profile` and no `--config`,
pycmdcheck runs every check that is installed and enabled. That is all 20
built-in checks, plus any [custom checks](custom-checks.qmd) installed in the
same environment. The deprecated [`imports`](#imports-check) check is left
out.

Such a run executes code from the project. It runs the test suite and the
doctests, builds the package, and requests each project URL over the network.
It also starts the linter, the type checker and the formatter that the project
has configured. A project that has configured none gets a skipped result for
that check, as [Configuration](configuration.qmd#tool-auto) explains. Make
such a run from the project's own environment, with the package and its tools
installed. [Getting Started](getting-started.qmd#tools-the-checks-need) lists
the tools.

To read files only, name a profile that does so.

```bash
pycmdcheck --profile triage
```

## Options

| Option | Default | What it does |
|--------|---------|--------------|
| `-c, --check NAME` | not set | Run only the named checks. Separate the names with commas or repeat the option. See [Selecting Checks](#selecting-checks). |
| `-s, --skip NAME` | not set | Skip the named checks. Separate the names with commas or repeat the option. See [Selecting Checks](#selecting-checks). |
| `--profile NAME` | not set | Use a named set of checks. See [Profiles](#profiles). |
| `--config FILE` | not set | Take the profile, the checks and their options from `FILE`, a settings file kept outside the directory that is checked. See [`--config`](#config-file). |
| `--fail-on STATUS` | the `fail_on` of the `--config` file when one is given, else the `fail_on` list in `pyproject.toml`, or `error` | Exit with code 1 when a check returns this status or a more severe one. See [`--fail-on`](#fail-on). |
| `--exit-zero` | off | Exit with code 0 whatever the checks find. |
| `-x, --fail-fast` | off | Start no further check after the first error. |
| `--no-parallel` | off | Run one check at a time. |
| `-v, --verbose` | off | Add a Time column, and show the detail lines of each check and a suggestion for each finding. See [Text Output](#text-output). |
| `--format FORMAT` | `text` | Print the report as `text`, `json` or `markdown`. See [Output](#output). |
| `--json` | off | Print the report as JSON. The same as `--format json`. |
| `--output FILE` | standard output | Write the report or listing to `FILE` and print nothing on standard output. See [`--output`](#output-file). |
| `--list` | | List the installed checks and exit. |
| `--list-profiles` | | List the profiles, with their checks and the options they set, and exit. |
| `--list-rules` | | List the rules of every installed check, with their codes and a suggestion for each, and exit. See [`--list-rules`](#list-rules). |
| `--install-skill [DIR]` | `.claude/skills` for `DIR` | Copy the skill for AI assistants that this version carries to `DIR/pycmdcheck` and exit. See [`--install-skill`](#install-skill). |
| `--debug` | off | Print debug logging on standard error. |
| `--version` | | Print the version and exit. |
| `-h, --help` | | Print the help text and exit. |

### Selecting Checks

`--check` runs only the checks you name, in the order you name them. `--skip`,
or `-s` for short, removes checks from whatever would otherwise run. Each
takes one name, or several names separated by commas with no space after a
comma.

```bash
# Two checks only
pycmdcheck --check metadata,license

# A profile without two of its checks
pycmdcheck --profile triage --skip citation,community
```

Each option can also be repeated, and the two forms can be mixed.
`--check tests,linting --check formatting` selects the same three checks as
`--check tests,linting,formatting`. A name that is given twice counts once.

An unknown name given to `--check` or to `--skip` is a usage error with exit
code 2, and no check runs. A misspelled name after `--skip` would otherwise
leave in the check it was meant to take out. This is the last line that
`pycmdcheck --profile triage --skip licence` writes to standard error.

```
Error: Unknown check(s) given to --skip: licence. Available checks: build, changelog, ci, citation, community, dependencies, docs, doctests, formatting, imports, license, linting, metadata, py_typed, python_versions, structure, test_suite, tests, typing, urls, version
```

A value that holds no name is a usage error of the same kind. That is an
empty value, or one made of commas and spaces only. `pycmdcheck --check ""`
ends with this line.

```
Error: --check needs at least one check name.
```

A value with an empty name beside others, such as `license,`, is a usage
error too. The usual cause is a space after a comma. The shell splits
`--check license, docs` into the value `license,` and the word `docs`, and
pycmdcheck takes `docs` as `PATH`, the directory to check. In a project that
has a `docs` directory, the command ends with this line.

```
Error: --check has an empty name in "license,". Write the names with commas and no spaces, as in tests,linting.
```

In a project that has no such directory, the last line is about `PATH` and
does not name the option.

```
Error: Invalid value for '[PATH]': Directory 'docs' does not exist.
```

Quotes keep the value in one piece, and the spaces around a name are then
ignored. So `--check "metadata, license"` works. With `--skip`, the line for
a value that holds no name and the line for an empty name start with
`Error: --skip`.

A `--skip` that takes out every check the run would hold is a usage error
too. Those are the checks named with `--check`, or else the checks of the
profile, or else every installed check that is not deprecated and that the
project has not turned off in `[tool.pycmdcheck.checks]`.
`pycmdcheck --check docs --skip docs` ends with this line.

```
Error: --skip leaves no check to run.
```

A project that sets every check to `false` leaves nothing for `--skip` to
take out. A run with no `--check` and no profile then prints a report with
no results and the line `No checks were run.`, and the exit code is 0, with
or without `--skip`.

Two cases are more lenient. A run that only prints a listing, with `--list`,
`--list-profiles` or `--list-rules`, does not look at the values given to
`--check` and `--skip`. Neither an unknown name nor an empty one is an error
there. In Python, `check()` and `run_checks()` ignore an unknown name in
`skip` and log a warning, and a `skip` list that leaves no check gives an
empty report.

Which way to choose the checks depends on what you need.

| Need | Use | Example |
|-------------|-------------|----------------|
| A few checks, once | `--check` | `pycmdcheck --check metadata,license` |
| A built-in set of checks | [`--profile`](#profiles) | `pycmdcheck --profile triage` |
| A built-in set without some of its checks | `--profile` with `--skip` | `pycmdcheck --profile triage --skip citation,community` |
| The same set on every run, kept in a file outside the project | [`--config`](#config-file) | `pycmdcheck --config triage.toml path/to/repo` |
| Settings for your own package | The `[tool.pycmdcheck]` table in its `pyproject.toml`, which [Configuration](configuration.qmd) describes | `pycmdcheck` |

### Profiles

A profile is a named set of checks. Some profiles also set check options.

| Profile | Checks | Options it sets |
|---------|--------|-----------------|
| `minimal` | `license`, `metadata`, `structure` | none |
| `triage` | The 12 checks that only read files, which are `changelog`, `ci`, `citation`, `community`, `docs`, `license`, `metadata`, `py_typed`, `python_versions`, `structure`, `test_suite` and `version` | `docs` gets `require_readme = true`, `check_readme_sections = true`, `check_docs_site = true`, `check_docstrings = false` and `min_docstring_coverage = 0` |
| `core` | 13 checks, which are `build`, `dependencies`, `docs`, `formatting`, `license`, `linting`, `metadata`, `py_typed`, `structure`, `test_suite`, `tests`, `typing` and `version` | none |
| `default` | The same 13 checks. This is the old name of `core`. | none |
| `pyopensci` | All 20 built-in checks | `docs` gets `require_readme = true`, `check_docstrings = true`, `check_readme_sections = true`, `check_docs_site = true` and `min_docstring_coverage = 50` |
| `strict` | All 20 built-in checks | `docs` gets `require_readme = true`, `check_docstrings = true`, `check_readme_sections = true`, `check_docs_site = true` and `min_docstring_coverage = 80`. `linting` gets `tool = "ruff"`. `typing` gets `tool = "mypy"` and `strict = true`. |

You cannot define a named profile of your own, because a name that is not
built in would have to be looked up in the repository being checked. A
[`--config`](#config-file) file is the place for a selection of your own.

The name `default` is deprecated. It still works, and every run that uses it
prints this warning on standard error.

```
The profile name 'default' is deprecated. Use 'core' instead.
```

The `core` profile is not what runs when no profile is given. A run with no
profile executes every enabled check, as described under
[What a Run Executes](#what-a-run-executes).

Only `minimal` and `triage` are limited to reading files. The `core`,
`pyopensci` and `strict` profiles include checks that execute the project's
code and need its tools installed.

The `strict` profile names its tools. It lints with ruff and type checks with
`mypy --strict` on every project, also on one that has configured neither
tool or has chosen another one in `pyproject.toml`. Under every other profile
the `linting` and `typing` checks run the tool the project has configured and
are skipped when it has configured none. The `formatting` check works that
way under every profile, `strict` included.

The `triage` profile sets all five options of the `docs` check, and `docs`
is the only one of its 12 checks that has options. The `[tool.pycmdcheck]`
table of a checked project can therefore change no result of a triage run.
[Checking Untrusted Code](triage.qmd#what-the-profile-runs-and-leaves-out)
says what that table can still reach.

`pycmdcheck --list-profiles` prints the profiles of the installed version.
Each profile has a row for its checks, which starts with `Runs`, and a row
for each option it sets, which starts with `Sets`. These are the first lines
of the output at a width of 72 columns. The other four profiles follow in
the same form.

```
                           Available Profiles
┏━━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓
┃ Name      ┃ Description, checks and options                          ┃
┡━━━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┩
│ minimal   │ Quick basic checks (metadata, structure, license)        │
│           │ Runs license, metadata, structure                        │
├───────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ triage    │ Static checks that only read files. No install, external │
│           │ tools, or network (for CI triage of arbitrary            │
│           │ repositories)                                            │
│           │ Runs changelog, ci, citation, community, docs, license,  │
│           │ metadata, py_typed, python_versions, structure,          │
│           │ test_suite, version                                      │
│           │ Sets docs.require_readme = true                          │
│           │ Sets docs.check_readme_sections = true                   │
│           │ Sets docs.check_docs_site = true                         │
│           │ Sets docs.check_docstrings = false                       │
│           │ Sets docs.min_docstring_coverage = 0                     │
```

With `--json` the listing is a JSON array with one object for each profile.
An object has the four keys `name`, `description`, `checks` and `options`.
This is the first of the six objects.

```json
{
  "name": "minimal",
  "description": "Quick basic checks (metadata, structure, license)",
  "checks": [
    "license",
    "metadata",
    "structure"
  ],
  "options": {}
}
```

`options` has one entry for each check whose options the profile sets, and
it is empty for a profile that sets none. This is the key in the object for
`triage`.

```json
"options": {
  "docs": {
    "require_readme": true,
    "check_readme_sections": true,
    "check_docs_site": true,
    "check_docstrings": false,
    "min_docstring_coverage": 0
  }
}
```

In Python, `pycmdcheck.profiles.get_profile("triage")` returns the profile.
Its attributes `checks` and `config_overrides` hold the check names and the
options. `list_profiles()` in the same module returns only the name and the
description of each profile.

### `--config` {#config-file}

`--config FILE` takes the profile, the checks and their options from `FILE`,
a settings file that you keep outside the directory that is checked. With
this option the `[tool.pycmdcheck]` table of the checked directory is not
read at all. The option is new in version 0.2.0.

The option is for checking repositories you do not own, as a review bot does,
or an organization that holds all its packages to one standard. You cannot
put settings into those repositories, and their own settings should not
change your run.

For most such needs a built-in profile trimmed on the command line is enough.

```bash
pycmdcheck --profile triage --skip citation --fail-on error path/to/repo
```

A settings file is worth having when that line grows, or when an option of a
check has to be set from outside the repository. The file is written in TOML
(Tom's Obvious Minimal Language), the format of `pyproject.toml`. This one
runs the `triage` profile without `citation` and makes the run fail on
warnings as well as on errors.

```toml
# .github/pycmdcheck-triage.toml, in the bot's own repository
profile = "triage"
fail_on = "warning"

[checks]
citation = false
```

```bash
pycmdcheck --config .github/pycmdcheck-triage.toml path/to/repo
```

These are the first lines of the report for the small package from
[Getting Started](getting-started.qmd#your-first-check). The first line names
the file beside the profile, without its directory, and the table has no
`citation` row. The path is shortened here.

```
Checking package: .../riverplot (profile: triage, config: pycmdcheck-triage.toml)

┏━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓
┃     ┃ Check           ┃ Message                                     ┃
┡━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┩
│  ✓  │ changelog       │ Changelog present                           │
│  ℹ  │ ci              │ No CI configuration found                   │
│  ℹ  │ community       │ 2 community file(s) not found in repository │
```

The Markdown report names the file in the same way, and the JSON report
gives the path in its `config_file` key.

The file follows four rules.
[Configuration](configuration.qmd#config-file) is the reference for its
keys, for the options it may set and for its error messages.

- `profile` names one built-in profile. The key is required.
- Under `[checks]` the file can take a check out of the profile and set
  options for a check that is in it. It cannot add a check.
- `fail_on` is the threshold of the run, as [`--fail-on`](#fail-on) is. The
  default is `error`.
- The options are checked strictly. An unknown option, a value of the wrong
  type and a value out of range are each an error.

pycmdcheck does not test where the file is kept. Keep it where the checked
repository cannot change it.

The other options work next to `--config` as follows.

| Option | With `--config` |
|--------|-----------------|
| `--profile` | A usage error. The file names the profile. |
| `--check NAME` | Narrows the run to the named checks. Each has to be a check the file runs. A check outside the profile is a usage error, and so is one the file took out. |
| `--skip NAME` | Takes more checks out. When no check is left, that is a usage error, as it is [without `--config`](#selecting-checks). |
| `--fail-on` | Wins over the `fail_on` of the file |
| `--exit-zero` | Keeps the exit code at 0 whatever the checks find, as in every run |

Each usage error in this table writes a last line of its own to standard
error. These three come from runs with the file above. The first run added
`--profile triage`, the second `--check tests`, and the third
`--check license --skip license`.

```
Error: --config cannot be used with --profile. The config file names the profile.
Error: Check(s) not run by the config file: tests. It runs changelog, ci, community, docs, license, metadata, py_typed, python_versions, structure, test_suite, version
Error: --skip leaves no check to run.
```

A mistake in the file is a usage error with exit code 2. It is found before
any check runs. Nothing is written to standard output or to the `--output`
file, and `--exit-zero` does not change the code. The last line on standard
error names the file as it was given and says what is wrong. Each of these
three lines comes from a run of its own. The mistakes are a check that is
not in the profile, an option value of the wrong type, and a misspelled
check name.

```
Error: Config file .github/pycmdcheck-triage.toml: tests is not in the profile triage. A config file can take a check out of a profile and cannot add one.
Error: Config file .github/pycmdcheck-triage.toml: docs.check_docstrings must be true or false, but it is "no".
Error: Config file .github/pycmdcheck-triage.toml: Unknown check citaton in [checks]. The profile triage holds changelog, ci, citation, community, docs, license, metadata, py_typed, python_versions, structure, test_suite, version.
```

The file is read before a listing is printed as well. So
`pycmdcheck --config FILE --list` tests a file with no repository at hand.
When the file is sound, it prints the usual list of every installed check,
not the checks the file selects. When it is not, it prints the error line.
`--list-profiles` and `--list-rules` read the file in the same way.

### The Deprecated imports Check {#imports-check}

Version 0.2.0 merged the `imports` check into `dependencies`, which reports
undeclared imports from the same scan. The name `imports` stays registered
for one release, so `--list` still shows it. It is in no profile, and a run
with no `--check` leaves it out. It runs only when `--check` names it, and
then it is always skipped. Because the name is registered, `--skip imports`
is accepted as well and is not an unknown name. Take `imports` out of
`--skip` now all the same. Once the name is removed, `--skip imports` is a
usage error with exit code 2.

```
│  ○  │ imports │ Merged into the dependencies check │
```

A project whose `[tool.pycmdcheck.checks]` table still enables `imports`,
with `imports = true` or with a table of its own, gets this warning on
standard error in a run with no `--check` and no profile. Delete the entry to
make it go away.

```
The deprecated check(s) enabled in [tool.pycmdcheck.checks] were left out: imports
```

### Precedence

The command line, the profile and `pyproject.toml` can each say which checks
run. They are applied in this order.

1. `--check` decides. The profile's check set and the enable flags in
   `pyproject.toml` are then not consulted.
2. Without `--check`, the profile's check set decides. The enable flags in
   `pyproject.toml` are not consulted, so `license = false` does not take
   `license` out of a profile.
3. With neither, every installed check runs unless `pyproject.toml` sets it to
   `false`. The deprecated `imports` check is the exception. It stays out
   whatever `pyproject.toml` says.
4. `--skip` then removes checks from the set that was chosen.

Check options follow one rule. An option set by the profile wins over the same
option in `pyproject.toml`, and every other option keeps its `pyproject.toml`
value. This holds when `--check` narrows the run as well. The profile then
supplies only its options, and the first line of the report ends with
`(options from profile: NAME)`.

Custom checks are outside every profile. A profile lists built-in checks only,
so a custom check runs in a run with no profile, or when `--check` names it.

This order is what makes a profile usable on a repository you did not write.
Its `pyproject.toml` cannot switch a check off or relax an option the profile
sets. It can still set [`fail_on`](configuration.qmd#fail_on), which counts
when `--fail-on` is not given, and any option the profile leaves alone.

A run with [`--config`](#config-file) has one more source, the settings
file, and loses one. The `[tool.pycmdcheck]` table of the checked directory
is not read, so that table has no say in what follows.

1. The file decides which checks can run. They are the checks of its profile
   without the ones the file takes out.
2. `--check` narrows the run to checks from that set. It cannot bring in a
   check from outside it, so a custom check never runs here.
3. `--skip` then removes checks.

The options of such a run are put together in three steps, and a later step
wins. First come the built-in defaults, then the options of the profile,
then the options of the file. The threshold comes from `--fail-on`, else
from the `fail_on` of the file, and is `error` when neither is given. When
`--check` narrows the run, the first line of the report ends with
`(options from profile: NAME, config: FILE)`.

### `--fail-on` {#fail-on}

The choices are `error`, `warning` and `note`. The option names a threshold.
The run exits with code 1 when a check returns that status or a more severe
one.

| Option | Statuses that fail the run |
|--------|----------------------------|
| `--fail-on error` | error |
| `--fail-on warning` | warning and error |
| `--fail-on note` | note, warning and error |

When the option is repeated, the least severe status counts. When it is not
given, pycmdcheck reads the [`fail_on`](configuration.qmd#fail_on) list from
`pyproject.toml` in the same way. A run with [`--config`](#config-file)
reads the `fail_on` of the settings file in its place. Without either
setting, only an error makes the run fail. A skipped check never fails the
run.

```bash
pycmdcheck --check license --fail-on warning
```

On a package with no license file, that run ends with these lines and exit
code 1. Without the option the closing line is `No errors (1 warning).` and
the exit code is 0. [Text Output](#text-output) explains the line that
follows the closing line.

```
│  ⚠  │ license │ No license file found │
└─────┴─────────┴───────────────────────┘

1 warning

Failed: 1 warning.
Run again with --verbose to see a suggestion for each finding.
```

### `--exit-zero` {#exit-zero}

With this option the exit code says whether pycmdcheck ran, not what it found.
Findings never produce exit code 1. Codes 2 and 3 are still used. It suits a
caller that reads the report itself, such as a continuous integration job that
parses the JSON.

```bash
pycmdcheck --profile triage --json --exit-zero > report.json
```

### `--fail-fast` {#fail-fast}

With `--fail-fast`, or `-x` for short, no check starts after the first one
that returns an error. Checks that are already running finish and keep their
results. Every check that was not started is reported as skipped with the
message `Not run (fail-fast)` and the skip reason `fail-fast`, so the report
still lists every selected check. Only an error triggers this, whatever
`--fail-on` says.

These are the last lines of a report from
`pycmdcheck --profile triage --fail-fast --no-parallel`, for a package whose
`pyproject.toml` does not parse.

```
│  ✓  │ license         │ License file present                        │
│  ✗  │ metadata        │ Invalid pyproject.toml                      │
│  ○  │ py_typed        │ Not run (fail-fast)                         │
│  ○  │ python_versions │ Not run (fail-fast)                         │
│  ○  │ structure       │ Not run (fail-fast)                         │
│  ○  │ test_suite      │ Not run (fail-fast)                         │
│  ○  │ version         │ Not run (fail-fast)                         │
└─────┴─────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

3 ok | 3 note | 1 error | 5 skipped

Failed: 1 error.
Run again with --verbose to see a suggestion for each finding.
```

### `--no-parallel`

By default up to four checks run at the same time. With this option they run
one after another. The report lists the results in the same order either way.
With `--fail-fast`, running one at a time also fixes which checks are skipped.

### `--list` and `--list-profiles`

`--list` prints every installed check with its description, custom checks
included. It does not show what a given profile or `--check` would select.
`--list-profiles` prints each profile with its description, its checks and
the options it sets.

With `--json`, `--list` prints a JSON array of objects that have a `name` and
a `description`. The objects of `--list-profiles` have those two keys, the
list `checks` and the object `options`. With `--format markdown` each prints
the same table as without it. Both honor [`--output`](#output-file) and then
write the listing to the file.

```bash
pycmdcheck --list
pycmdcheck --list-profiles --json
```

[Getting Started](getting-started.qmd#built-in-checks) shows the output of
`--list`, and [Profiles](#profiles) shows that of `--list-profiles`.

### `--list-rules` {#list-rules}

`--list-rules` prints every rule of every installed check, custom checks
included, and runs no check. A rule has a [code](rules.qmd) and a description
of what it reports. Every rule that comes with pycmdcheck also has a hint,
which is one sentence that says what to do about a finding of that rule. A
rule of a [custom check](custom-checks.qmd#hints) can have none. On the
terminal and in the Markdown report a hint comes after the label
`Suggestion:`, so a suggestion and a hint are the same thing.

The text output is a list and not a table. It starts with the line `Rules`.
Each rule comes after an empty line. Its first line gives the code and, in
parentheses, the check. The description is next, and the hint follows it
after `Suggestion:`. Both are indented by two spaces. A long line is wrapped
between words to the width of the terminal, and the rest of it continues
four spaces in. A rule with no hint has no `Suggestion:` line. The rules are
sorted by code. These are the first lines of the output at a width of 80
columns.

```
Rules

build.could-not-run (build)
  The build module is installed but could not run
  Suggestion: Run python -m build with the same args in the project directory
    and fix the error it prints.

build.failed (build)
  The package does not build
  Suggestion: Run python -m build in the project directory and fix the first
    error it prints.

build.invalid-args (build)
  The args option is not a list of strings
  Suggestion: Write args as a list with one string for each argument, so
    "--wheel --sdist" becomes ["--wheel", "--sdist"].
```

With `--json` the listing is a JSON array of objects that have the four keys
`check`, `code`, `description` and `hint`. `hint` is `null` for a rule that
has none. The option honors [`--output`](#output-file) as well.

```bash
pycmdcheck --list-rules --json
```

These are the first two of the objects.

```json
[
  {
    "check": "build",
    "code": "build.could-not-run",
    "description": "The build module is installed but could not run",
    "hint": "Run python -m build with the same args in the project directory and fix the error it prints."
  },
  {
    "check": "build",
    "code": "build.failed",
    "description": "The package does not build",
    "hint": "Run python -m build in the project directory and fix the first error it prints."
  }
]
```

The four rules of pycmdcheck itself are listed under the check name
`pycmdcheck`. The listing does not say which status a rule carries.
[Rule Codes](rules.qmd#rules-of-each-check) has that for the built-in checks.

A report can give a more exact hint than the listing gives for the same code.
A check writes the hint of a finding itself when the advice depends on what
it found. The listing gives `py_typed.missing` the hint
`Add an empty file named py.typed to the package directory.` A report names
the directory, as in `Add an empty file named py.typed to src/riverplot.`

### `--install-skill` {#install-skill}

`--install-skill` copies the skill that this version of pycmdcheck carries
into a skills directory and exits. The skill is a file of instructions for
an AI assistant, and [With an AI Assistant](assistants.qmd) says what it
does. The option is new in version 0.2.0 and has no short form.

```bash
pycmdcheck --install-skill
```

```
Installed the skill in .claude/skills/pycmdcheck/SKILL.md.
```

The skill goes to `DIR/pycmdcheck/SKILL.md`. Without `DIR` the skills
directory is `.claude/skills` in the current directory. Missing directories
are made, and other files in the folder are left alone. A second run writes
nothing and prints
`The skill in .claude/skills/pycmdcheck/SKILL.md is already up to date.` A
copy that differs is replaced without a question, and the line then starts
with `Updated`. That keeps the copy in step with the installed version, and
an edit made by hand is lost.

The last part of `DIR` must be named `skills`, as in `~/.claude/skills` or
`.agents/skills`. Any other name is a usage error with exit code 2, and
nothing is written. The option takes the next word as `DIR`, so without this
rule `pycmdcheck --install-skill mypackage` would write a folder into the
package it was meant to check. The command ends with this line.

```
Error: --install-skill read "mypackage" as its directory. The directory must be named skills, as in .claude/skills.
```

A write that fails is a usage error with exit code 2. So is a symbolic link
at `DIR/pycmdcheck` or at the `SKILL.md` in it, and then nothing is written.

```
Error: Nothing was written because .claude/skills/pycmdcheck is a symbolic link, so remove the link or pick another directory.
```

The option runs no check and reads no settings.

## Output

`--format` chooses the form of the report.

| Format | What it prints |
|--------|----------------|
| `text` | A table for the terminal. This is the default. |
| `json` | One JSON object for another program to read. `--json` means the same. |
| `markdown` | A report to post as a comment on a pull request or an issue |

`--json` together with `--format text` or `--format markdown` is a usage
error.

The report goes to standard output, or to the file that
[`--output`](#output-file) names. Warnings, such as a note that
`pyproject.toml` could not be read, go to standard error, and so do usage
errors and debug logging. Standard output therefore holds nothing but the
report, and with `--json` it can be redirected to a file and parsed. The text
report begins before the checks run, with a line that names the directory.
JSON and Markdown are printed in one piece when the run is over.

### Text Output {#text-output}

After its first line, the text report has a table with one row for each
check, a line with the counts, and a closing line. The closing line follows
the same rule as the exit code, and it reads the same with `--exit-zero`. The
table below gives its three forms, and the first row that applies is used.

| Closing line | When |
|--------------|------|
| `Failed: 1 error, 4 notes.` | A check returned the `--fail-on` status or a more severe one. The causes are listed from most to least severe. |
| `No errors (1 warning, 2 skipped).` | There are warnings, or checks that could not look, for example because a tool or a prerequisite is missing |
| `All checks passed!` | Every result is ok or a note. A check skipped because the project gave it nothing to look at does not count against this line |

The table of checks does not show the [hints](#list-rules), which say what to
do about each finding. When at least one finding has a hint, one more line
follows the closing line, and it points to `--verbose`, or `-v` for short.
These are the last lines of `pycmdcheck --check license,py_typed` on the
small package from [Getting Started](getting-started.qmd#your-first-check).

```
│  ✓  │ license  │ License file present                      │
│  ℹ  │ py_typed │ Missing py.typed marker for typed package │
└─────┴──────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────┘

1 ok | 1 note

All checks passed!
Run again with --verbose to see a suggestion for each finding.
```

`--verbose` adds a Time column to the table, with the seconds each check
took. Below the table it prints a block for each check that has detail lines
or hints. The block starts with the name of the check, as in
`py_typed details:`. The detail lines come first. They say what the check
looked for and what it found. One `Suggestion:` line follows for each hint,
and findings that have the same hint share a line. Each line of a block is
indented by two spaces. A line that is too long for the terminal is wrapped
between words, and the rest of it continues four spaces in, as the listing
of [`--list-rules`](#list-rules) shows. A detail line that has an indent of
its own keeps it, and the rest of such a line goes two spaces further in.
The line that points to `--verbose` is left out. This is the same run with
`--verbose`, from the table on.

```
┏━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━┓
┃     ┃ Check    ┃ Message                                   ┃  Time ┃
┡━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━┩
│  ✓  │ license  │ License file present                      │ 0.00s │
│  ℹ  │ py_typed │ Missing py.typed marker for typed package │ 0.00s │
└─────┴──────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────┴───────┘

license details:
  Found license file: LICENSE
  License type: MIT
  License is OSI-approved (MIT)

py_typed details:
  Package directory: src/riverplot
  Scanned 2 of 2 files: 2 of 2 public functions are annotated
  Suggestion: Add an empty file named py.typed to src/riverplot.

1 ok | 1 note

All checks passed!
```

A check whose result is ok has no finding and so no hint, as `license` shows.
The same holds for a skipped check. Its detail lines can still say what would
let the check run, such as which tool to install.

The JSON and Markdown reports always hold the hints, so neither has a line
that points to `--verbose`.

### `--output` {#output-file}

`--output FILE` writes the report to `FILE` as UTF-8, in the format that
`--format` chose, and prints nothing on standard output. An existing file is
replaced. Warnings still go to standard error.

```bash
pycmdcheck --profile triage --format markdown --output report.md
```

The file name is tested before any check runs. An empty name, a name that is
a directory, and a file in a directory that does not exist are each a usage
error with exit code 2. `--output -` means standard output. The option also
applies to `--list`, `--list-profiles` and `--list-rules`.

### JSON Output

`--json` prints one JSON object with twelve keys.

| Key | Type | Meaning |
|-----|------|---------|
| `package_path` | string | Absolute path of the directory that was checked |
| `passed` | boolean | `true` when no check returned `error`. It does not look at `--fail-on`. |
| `summary` | object | Number of results for each of `ok`, `note`, `warning`, `error` and `skipped` |
| `results` | array | One object for each check, in the order the terminal table uses |
| `schema_version` | integer | Version of this layout. It is `1`. |
| `pycmdcheck_version` | string | Version of pycmdcheck that wrote the report |
| `profile` | string or `null` | The name given to `--profile`, or the profile that the `--config` file names. `null` when neither option was given. |
| `config_file` | string or `null` | The file given to `--config`, as it was written on the command line, or `null` when none was given |
| `fail_on` | array of strings | The statuses that fail the run once the threshold rule is applied, most severe first |
| `failed` | boolean | `true` when a check returned one of the statuses in `fail_on`. This is the rule for exit code 1, and `--exit-zero` does not change the value. |
| `requested_checks` | array of strings or `null` | The names given with `--check`, one in each string, or `null` when there were none |
| `skipped_checks` | array of strings | The names given with `--skip`, one in each string. Empty when there were none. |

The last eight keys are new in version 0.2.0. `passed` and `failed` answer
different questions. With `--fail-on warning`, a report with one warning and
no error has `passed` and `failed` both set to `true`.

A check that a `--config` file took out is named nowhere in the report. It
is absent from `results`, and `skipped_checks` holds only the names given
with `--skip`.

Each entry of `results` has seven keys. The last two are new in version
0.2.0.

| Key | Type | Meaning |
|-----|------|---------|
| `name` | string | The check name, as shown by `--list` |
| `status` | string | One of `ok`, `note`, `warning`, `error`, `skipped` |
| `message` | string | One line that says what the check concluded |
| `details` | array of strings | What the check looked for and what it found. A skipped result may also say here what would let the check run. |
| `duration` | number | Seconds the check took |
| `findings` | array of objects | What the check found, in a form a program can read. Empty when the status is `ok` or `skipped`. |
| `skip_reason` | string or `null` | Why a skipped check did not look at anything. `null` for every other status. |

Each entry of `findings` has four keys.

| Key | Type | Meaning |
|-----|------|---------|
| `code` | string | The rule the finding comes from, such as `community.missing-contributing` |
| `status` | string | One of `note`, `warning`, `error` |
| `message` | string | One line that says what was found |
| `hint` | string or `null` | One sentence that says what to do about the finding, or `null` when the check gives none. Every finding of a built-in check has one. |

The status of a result is that of its most severe finding. The `message` of a
result and of a finding, the `details` and the `hint` are written for people
and their wording can change. The codes and the skip reasons are stable, and
[Rule Codes](rules.qmd) lists them all.

This is the output of `pycmdcheck --profile triage --json --exit-zero` on a
small package. The path is shortened, and 10 of the 12 results are left out.

```json
{
  "package_path": ".../riverplot",
  "passed": true,
  "summary": {
    "ok": 7,
    "note": 5,
    "warning": 0,
    "error": 0,
    "skipped": 0
  },
  "results": [
    {
      "name": "changelog",
      "status": "ok",
      "message": "Changelog present",
      "details": [
        "Found: CHANGELOG.md"
      ],
      "duration": 0.0010368824005126953,
      "findings": [],
      "skip_reason": null
    },
    {
      "name": "community",
      "status": "note",
      "message": "2 community file(s) not found in repository",
      "details": [
        "Not found in repository (root, .github/, docs/, doc/): CONTRIBUTING.md, CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md",
        "Organization-level default community health files cannot be detected by this check"
      ],
      "duration": 0.0018780231475830078,
      "findings": [
        {
          "code": "community.missing-contributing",
          "status": "note",
          "message": "CONTRIBUTING.md not found in repository",
          "hint": "Add a CONTRIBUTING.md file to the project root or .github/ that says how to report problems and send changes."
        },
        {
          "code": "community.missing-code-of-conduct",
          "status": "note",
          "message": "CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md not found in repository",
          "hint": "Add a CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md file to the project root or .github/, with a text such as the Contributor Covenant."
        }
      ],
      "skip_reason": null
    }
  ],
  "schema_version": 1,
  "pycmdcheck_version": "0.2.0",
  "profile": "triage",
  "config_file": null,
  "fail_on": [

  "failed": false,
  "requested_checks": null,
  "skipped_checks": []

```

### Markdown Output {#markdown-output}

`--format markdown` prints a report that can be posted as a comment. It has
five parts.

1. A heading.
2. One line with the name of the directory, the profile and the pycmdcheck
   version. Only the last part of the path is shown. With `--config` the
   line also gives the name of the settings file, as in
   `(profile: triage, config: pycmdcheck-triage.toml)`.
3. A table with one row for each check.
4. A line in bold with the counts and the closing line of the text report.
5. One collapsed block for each result that is not ok and has detail lines
   or [hints](#text-output). The block is a list. The detail lines come
   first, and one item that starts with `**Suggestion:**` follows for each
   hint. With `--verbose`, a result that is ok and has detail lines gets a
   block as well.

This is the output of `pycmdcheck --profile triage --format markdown` on the
same small package. Four of the five collapsed blocks are left out.

```markdown
## pycmdcheck report

Checked riverplot (profile: triage) with pycmdcheck 0.2.0.

| Status | Check | Message |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ok | changelog | Changelog present |
| note | ci | No CI configuration found |
| note | citation | No citation file found |
| note | community | 2 community file(s) not found in repository |
| note | docs | Some documentation improvements suggested |
| ok | license | License file present |
| ok | metadata | Package metadata is valid |
| note | py\_typed | Missing py.typed marker for typed package |
| ok | python\_versions | Python version requirement is current |
| ok | structure | Valid src layout structure |
| ok | test\_suite | Test suite present |
| ok | version | Version 0.3.0 is consistent |

**7 ok, 5 note. All checks passed!**

<details>
<summary>community: note</summary>

- Not found in repository (root, .github/, docs/, doc/): CONTRIBUTING.md, CODE\_OF\_CONDUCT.md
- Organization-level default community health files cannot be detected by this check
- **Suggestion:** Add a CONTRIBUTING.md file to the project root or .github/ that says how to report problems and send changes.
- **Suggestion:** Add a CODE\_OF\_CONDUCT.md file to the project root or .github/, with a text such as the Contributor Covenant.

</details>
```

Messages, detail lines and hints often quote the checked project, and the
directory name belongs to it. The report therefore treats that text, the
check names and the name of a `--config` file as text to be shown and not as
Markdown to be read.

- Each piece of text is put on one line.
- The characters that Markdown reads as markup get a backslash in front. That
  is why the example shows `py\_typed`. A message cannot break the table,
  write a Markdown link or image, or start a heading.
- A zero-width space, which is an invisible character, follows every `@` and
  the first colon of anything shaped like `:word:`. GitHub then sends no
  notification to a user or a team and shows no emoji.
- The same character is placed inside the start of a web address, after
  `https:` or `www`. GitHub then shows the address as text and not as a link.
- A detail line that begins like a list item or a horizontal rule gets a
  backslash, so it stays one line of the list.

GitHub may still link a few kinds of plain text, such as an issue reference
written as `GH-1`.

Text copied from the rendered comment can carry the invisible character. A
location such as `mod.py:100: error` is one example. Use `--json` for
anything a program reads.
[Checking Untrusted Code](triage.qmd#posting-a-comment) shows the report in
use.

### When a Check Is Skipped

A skipped check did not look at anything, so it gave no verdict. Its message
says why in words, and the `skip_reason` key of the JSON report says it with
one of nine fixed values. The usual reasons are that a tool is not installed,
that the project has not configured a tool for the check, that the project
has nothing for the check to look at, that another check already reports what
is missing, or that `--fail-fast` stopped the run.
[Rule Codes](rules.qmd#skip-reasons) lists the values. A skipped check never
fails the run.

This is `pycmdcheck --check formatting,linting,typing` on a package that has
configured no formatter, no linter and no type checker.

```
│  ○  │ formatting │ No formatter configured    │
│  ○  │ linting    │ No linter configured       │
│  ○  │ typing     │ No type checker configured │
└─────┴────────────┴────────────────────────────┘

3 skipped

No errors (3 skipped).
```

In the JSON report each of these three results has the `skip_reason`
`not-configured`.

## Exit Codes

| Code | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| 0 | No check returned the `--fail-on` status or a more severe one. With `--exit-zero`, any set of results. |
| 1 | At least one check returned the `--fail-on` status or a more severe one. |
| 2 | Usage error. Examples are an unknown option, an unknown or empty check name given to `--check` or `--skip`, a mistake in the [`--config`](#config-file) file, a `PATH` that is not a directory, `--json` together with another `--format`, and an `--output` file that cannot be used. The message goes to standard error, nothing is printed on standard output, and no check runs. |
| 3 | pycmdcheck itself failed. One line goes to standard error. With JSON, Markdown or `--output`, no report is written. With the text report on standard output, the first line, which names the directory being checked, may already be there. |

`--exit-zero` does not change codes 2 and 3.

One usage error comes after the checks have run. When the `--output` file
passed the test at the start and still cannot be written at the end, for
example because the disk is full, the exit code is 2 and the report is lost.

## Checking Code You Do Not Trust

The `tests`, `doctests` and `build` checks execute code from the project. The
`typing` and `linting` checks start tools that can load a plugin or run a
start-up hook named in the project's own configuration. The `urls` check
sends requests to the addresses the project lists. It leaves out local and
private hosts, and it still contacts any public host the project names. A run
with no profile includes all six, and so do the `pyopensci` and `strict`
profiles. The `core` profile includes `tests`, `build`, `typing` and
`linting`.

For a repository you have not reviewed, use `--profile triage`, which runs
none of these. A [`--config`](#config-file) file that names `triage` runs
none of them either, and it keeps the repository's own settings out of the
run. Start it with the `pycmdcheck` command, or with
`python -P -m pycmdcheck`, and pass the repository as `PATH`. Do not run
`python -m pycmdcheck` from inside the repository.
[Checking Untrusted Code](triage.qmd) gives the full command, the reasons, and
how to read the result.

## Examples

### Continuous Integration

```bash
# Fail the job on warnings and errors from the checks that read files
pycmdcheck --profile triage --fail-on warning

# Never fail the job on findings, and keep the report for a later step
pycmdcheck --profile triage --json --exit-zero > report.json

# Write a report that a later step posts as a comment
pycmdcheck --profile triage --format markdown --exit-zero --output report.md

# Check a repository you do not own with settings from a file of your own
pycmdcheck --config pycmdcheck-triage.toml --json --exit-zero path/to/repo > report.json
```

### Development

```bash
# A quick look at two checks, with their detail lines and suggestions
pycmdcheck --check metadata,license --verbose

# Everything that needs no tools
pycmdcheck --profile triage

# What can be run
pycmdcheck --list
```
